title: Learning Representations to Guide Pixel Diffusion Transformers

paper.title: Learning Representations to Guide Pixel Diffusion Transformers
paper.abstract:
Abstract Visual representations are largely developed for understanding, yet what makes them useful for generation remains unclear.
We study this question in pixel diffusion transformers and uncover two key insights.
First, better representation quality does not necessarily translate into greater generative utility, as externally aligned semantics can be progressively lost during pixel synthesis.
Second, architectural separation with specialized pixel decoders mainly redistributes semantic and spatial modeling, without necessarily yielding representations better suited to generation.
These insights suggest that a useful generative representation must be both properly formed and actively exploited .
Motivated by these insights, we introduce Representation Guidance (RG) , which directly forms and exploits internal representations while retaining a plain Transformer architecture.
A low-dimensional bottleneck forces generation-relevant information into a compact representation, which is then explicitly used to guide decoder generation by modifying the flow-matching target according to its induced prediction offset.
RG learns clearer semantic and spatial structure while scaling efficiently in both parameters and computation.
On ImageNet 256 × 256 256\times 256 , RG-L/16 with only 459M parameters outperforms substantially larger pixel diffusion transformers, while RG-XL/16 achieves an FID of 1.55.
RG further reaches an FID of 1.74 at 512 × 512 512\times 512 and extends to text-to-image generation, achieving 0.89 on GenEval and 87.1 on DPG-Bench.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Representation learning has been a central theme in computer vision ( Chen et al., 2020 ; He et al., 2020 ; Caron et al., 2021 ; He et al., 2022 ) . By transforming pixels into structured features, modern vision models have learned representations that transfer effectively across recognition tasks such as classification, detection, and segmentation ( Oquab et al., 2023 ; Siméoni et al., 2025 ) . Yet visual representations have been developed predominantly for understanding. Whether the same notion of a “good representation” applies to generation remains much less clear. Unlike recognition, which can discard much of the low-level image content once semantics are extracted, generation must organize global semantics and spatial structure while ultimately recovering every pixel. This raises a fundamental question: what makes a representation useful for visual generation? Figure 2: Our RG enables efficient scaling and better internal representations. (a) RG scales consistently from B to XL. It achieves lower FID with fewer parameters and FLOPs than plain-Transformer JiT baselines, while also outperforming pixel-specialized decoders at lower complexity. (b) RG learns clearer spatial structure and more localized semantic correspondence. Recent generative models have increasingly borrowed representations from pretrained vision encoders. One line of work improves the latent space in which generation operates, either by aligning autoencoder latents with pretrained features ( Yao et al., 2025 ; Leng et al., 2025 ; Yue et al., 2026 ) or by directly using such features as generative latents ( Zheng et al., 2026a ; Shi et al., 2026b ; Singh et al., 2026 ) . Another line aligns intermediate generative features with pretrained representations ( Yu et al., 2024 ; Wu et al., 2025 ; Wang et al., 2025b ; Singh et al., 2025 ) . While these approaches show that semantic representations can facilitate generative learning, they largely focus on what information a representation contains . For generation, this is only part of the problem: a representation may encode rich semantic and spatial structure, yet provide limited benefit if it is not properly formed for synthesis or if the generative process does not actually exploit it. We study this problem in pixel diffusion transformers (pDiTs) ( Chen et al., 2025c ; Yu et al., 2026 ) , where representation learning and image synthesis take place end-to-end from raw pixels rather than through a representation space predefined by an external autoencoder ( Rombach et al., 2022 ) . More importantly, JiT ( Li & He, 2026 ) shows that competitive pixel generation can be achieved with a plain Transformer, providing a simple setting for examining how internal representations emerge and interact with pixel synthesis. Our analysis of this setting reveals two key insights. • First, better representation quality does not necessarily translate into greater generative utility. Aligning an intermediate JiT layer with DINOv2 ( Oquab et al., 2023 ) substantially improves its semantic and spatial structure at the aligned layer. However, these gains rapidly diminish in subsequent layers as the network approaches pixel prediction. The same mismatch appears in generation: REPA ( Yu et al., 2024 ) accelerates early training, but the baseline eventually overtakes it, while moving the alignment deeper further degrades the final FID. These results show that simply injecting stronger semantics is insufficient—a representation benefits generation only when its information is preserved and remains functionally relevant to subsequent synthesis. • Second, architectural separation does not necessarily improve representation for generation; it mainly redistributes semantic and spatial modeling across the network. A natural response is to separate representation learning from pixel synthesis with an additional specialized pixel decoder ( Yu et al., 2026 ; Ma et al., 2026a ; Chen et al., 2026 ) . However, the decoder itself reshapes the encoder representation: its spatial modeling capacity determines what the encoder must retain, producing different balances of global semantics and spatial structure without yielding a representation better suited to generation. These designs also incur substantial parameter and computation overhead. Thus, they mainly shift the modeling burden between encoder and decoder while departing from JiT’s simple, scalable Transformer design. Figure 3: Architecture comparison. (a) JiT and (b) RG use patch-level input and standard Transformer blocks. JiT uses a single stack, while RG conditions its decoder on the bottleneck output, which is randomly dropped during training. (c)–(e) Pixel-specialized decoders take pixel-level input: patch attention with pixel-wise FFNs in PixelDiT, a pixel-wise MLP in DeCo, and a convolutional network with skip connections in DiP. Input tokens are noisy, output tokens are clean, and rounded squares denote the tokens output by the patch embedding or patch encoder. Together, these findings suggest that a useful generative representation must be both properly formed and actively exploited . It should emerge through a compact interface that encourages the model to organize information into a concise, generation-relevant representation, while remaining tightly coupled to subsequent synthesis. Neither alone is sufficient: forcing the generator to rely on a poorly formed representation can amplify unhelpful low-level information, whereas a well-structured representation provides little benefit if it can be ignored. Based on these insights, we introduce Representation Guidance (RG) . RG preserves a plain Transformer architecture and operates on the representation interface rather than introducing a specialized pixel decoder. First, a low-dimensional bottleneck between the encoder and decoder forms a compact implicit latent space, encouraging generation-relevant information to be organized into a concise internal representation. Second, RG explicitly strengthens the generative utility of this representation. We compare decoder predictions with and without the representation and use the resulting representation-induced velocity offset to modify the flow-matching target ( Lipman et al., 2023 ; Liu et al., 2023 ; Albergo & Vanden-Eijnden, 2023 ) . This increases the model’s dependence on the representation, while gradients through it simultaneously shape the encoder toward information useful for synthesis. The bottleneck and guidance thus play complementary roles: the former governs how the representation is formed , while the latter ensures that generation actually uses it . Pretrained representation alignment thus provides a semantic scaffold, while the representation consumed by the decoder is ultimately learned end-to-end for generation. RG also shares a core principle with self-distillation in self-supervised learning ( Caron et al., 2021 ; Oquab et al., 2023 ) : the representation is bootstrapped from targets derived from the model’s own predictions. Whereas self-distillation sharpens the teacher distribution to induce discriminative features, RG sharpens the velocity target along the representation-induced offset, which compels the representation to encode the semantic and spatial structure required for generation (Figure 6 ). Figure 2 summarizes the consequences of this representation-centered design. Without introducing specialized pixel modules, RG achieves a substantially stronger parameter–quality and compute–quality trade-off, scales consistently with model size, and develops markedly clearer semantic and spatial organization in its internal representations. On ImageNet ( Deng et al., 2009 ) 256 × 256 256\times 256 , RG-XL/16 achieves an FID of 1.55, while RG-L/16 reaches 1.79 with only 459M parameters, outperforming substantially larger pixel-space models. RG further achieves an FID of 1.74 at 512 × 512 512\times 512 and extends naturally to text-to-image generation, reaching 0.89 on GenEval ( Ghosh et al., 2023 ) and 87.1 on DPG-Bench ( Hu et al., 2024 ) . These results show that effective representation learning in pixel diffusion does not require increasingly elaborate pixel decoders or ever-stronger externally imposed features. Instead, a plain Transformer can learn representations that benefit generation when the representation is both properly formed and explicitly exploited.

sections.heading: 2 What Makes Representations Useful in pDiTs?
sections.text: We investigate how representations in pDiTs interact with generation. Our goal is not only to ask whether a representation becomes more semantic or spatially structured, but whether such improvements remain useful to the generative process. Unless otherwise specified, models in this section are base-sized and trained for 200 epochs on ImageNet 256 × 256 256\times 256 ( Deng et al., 2009 ) . We report FID-50K for generation quality, RMSC and LDS ( Singh et al., 2025 ) for spatial structure, and linear probing accuracy ( He et al., 2022 ) for global semantics. Appendix A.4 provides metric details. Baseline REPA-4 REPA-6 REPA-8 Figure 4: Representation quality does not necessarily translate into generative utility. REPA improves semantics and spatial structure at the aligned layer, but these gains quickly decay and do not improve final generation. REPA- k k aligns layer k k with DINOv2 features.

sections.heading: Does better representation quality translate into better generation?
sections.text: Pretrained representation alignment provides a direct way to strengthen the semantic and spatial structure of an intermediate representation. Rather than asking whether alignment can improve the aligned layer, we ask what happens afterwards: does this improvement survive subsequent pixel synthesis and benefit generation? We apply REPA ( Yu et al., 2024 ) at different layers of JiT-B/16 and track both the representation across layers and generation quality during training. • Experimental Results. Figure 4 reveals a clear mismatch. Aligning layer 4 substantially improves its RMSC, LDS, and linear probing accuracy, indicating stronger spatial structure and global semantics. However, these gains diminish immediately after the aligned layer as the network progresses toward pixel prediction. The same mismatch appears in generation: REPA-4 accelerates early training, but the baseline overtakes it after roughly 160 epochs and achieves a better final FID (4.56 vs. 4.80). Moreover, moving the alignment deeper further degrades generation, with FIDs of 5.38 and 8.33 for REPA-6 and REPA-8. • Analysis. These results suggest that later layers progressively overwrite externally imposed semantics as they specialize toward dense pixel interactions and high-frequency synthesis. This mirrors lazy aggregation in ViTs ( Shi et al., 2026a ) : models tend to follow the shortcut their supervision permits. As per-pixel supervision is largely satisfied by local operations, pDiTs lack incentive to form and exploit high-level representations. Alignment can therefore create a strong intermediate representation without making it useful to the final generative prediction; imposing it closer to the output can instead interfere more directly with pixel synthesis. Our first insight is that better representation quality does not necessarily translate into greater generative utility. A useful representation must remain functionally relevant throughout subsequent synthesis. Vanilla PixelDiT DiP DeCo Figure 5: Decoder design reshapes the encoder representation. Different pixel decoders induce different balances of global semantics and spatial structure in encoder. Vanilla and PixelDiT retain stronger global semantics, whereas DiP and DeCo preserve more structures but weaker semantics.

sections.heading: Does architectural separation yield a better representation for generation?
sections.text: A natural response to the above mismatch is to separate high-level representation learning from low-level synthesis with an additional, separately designed pixel decoder. Recent pDiTs follow this route using pixel-wise MLPs ( Ma et al., 2026a ) , convolutions ( Chen et al., 2026 ) , or pixel-level attention ( Yu et al., 2026 ) . But does such architectural separation actually produce a representation better suited to generation? We compare these designs under the same training budget and 𝐱 \mathbf{x} -prediction. • Experimental Results. Figure 5 shows that pixel-specialized decoders substantially reshape the encoder representation. Their linear probing accuracy drops sharply after the aligned layer and falls below that of the vanilla Transformer decoder. At the last encoder layer, DeCo and DiP retain stronger spatial variation but weaker global semantics, whereas vanilla and PixelDiT preserve stronger semantics but poor spatial structure. Consistently, Figure 2 (b) shows less spatially structured representations in PixelDiT than in RG. Table 1 shows that such specialization brings no consistent generation gain: PixelDiT roughly matches vanilla (4.26 vs. 4.17) with 55% more parameters and 67% more FLOPs, while DiP and DeCo reach FIDs of 6.09 and 9.17. • Analysis. These differences reflect what each decoder can model. Vanilla and PixelDiT capture cross-patch spatial relations in the decoder, allowing the encoder to focus more on global semantics. In contrast, DeCo and DiP process patches largely independently and therefore rely on the encoder to retain spatial information. The decoder thus does not merely consume the representation; its design changes what information the encoder must retain. Together with Table 1 , these results show that such redistribution does not consistently improve generation and often comes with higher parameter and computation costs. Our second insight is that architectural separation mainly redistributes semantic and spatial modeling rather than yielding a representation better suited to generation. Moreover, this specialization departs from JiT’s simple, scalable Transformer design. Table 1: Pixel-specialized decoders offer limited gains under the same training budget. sections.heading: Takeaways.
sections.text: Together, these findings motivate controlling both how the representation is formed during generation and how it is used by subsequent synthesis.

sections.heading: 4 Experiments
sections.text: We evaluate RG on class-conditional ImageNet generation ( Deng et al., 2009 ) and text-to-image generation. To study scalability, we instantiate RG with three model sizes: Base (B), Large (L), and Extra Large (XL). Table 9 summarizes their configurations. Unless otherwise specified, we use RG-B/16 trained for 200 epochs as the default model for all experiments on ImageNet.

sections.heading: Class-conditional image generation.
sections.text: We follow the training setup of JiT ( Li & He, 2026 ) on ImageNet-1K ( Deng et al., 2009 ) at 256 × 256 256\times 256 and 512 × 512 512\times 512 . We use AdamW with β = ( 0.9 , 0.95 ) \beta=(0.9,0.95) , a constant learning rate of 2 × 10 − 4 2\times 10^{-4} , a batch size of 1024, EMA with a decay of 0.9999, and bfloat16 mixed precision on 8 A100 GPUs. Timesteps follow a logit-normal distribution ( Esser et al., 2024 ) with logit ⁡ ( t ) ∼ 𝒩 ⁡ ( − 0.8 , 0.8 2 ) \operatorname{logit}(t)\sim\mathcal{N}(-0.8,0.8^{2}) . Unless otherwise stated, RG uses s = 1.4 s=1.4 and t min = 0.3 t_{\min}=0.3 and is enabled after 20 epochs. Following ADM ( Dhariwal & Nichol, 2021 ) , we report FID, Inception Score, precision, and recall on 50K samples. We sample with a 50-step Heun solver ( Heun, 1900 ) . CFG is applied only within a timestep interval ( Kynkäänniemi et al., 2024 ) .

sections.heading: Text-to-image generation.
sections.text: RG-T2I-L/16 replaces the JiT blocks of RG with the MM-JiT blocks of MiniT2I ( Wang et al., 2026b ) , which condition on text tokens from a frozen FLAN-T5-Large encoder ( Chung et al., 2022 ) . Following MiniT2I, the model is pretrained on CC12M ( Changpinyo et al., 2021 ) with LLaVA-NeXT captions ( Caption Emporium, 2024 ) and then fine-tuned on a 120K mixture of BLIP3o-60K ( Chen et al., 2025a ) , DALL-E 3 ( OpenDatasets, 2023 ) , and ShareGPT-4o-Image ( Chen et al., 2025b ) , both at 512 × 512 512\times 512 . We evaluate on GenEval ( Ghosh et al., 2023 ) and DPG-Bench ( Hu et al., 2024 ) , which contain 553 and 1,065 prompts. We generate 4 images per prompt with 100 sampling steps and a CFG scale of 5.0. To explore high-resolution generation, we further fine-tune the trained 512 × 512 512\times 512 model at 1024 × 1024 1024\times 1024 on curated internal data.

sections.heading: Class-conditional image generation on ImageNet.
sections.text: As shown in Table 2 , RG-XL/16 achieves an FID of 1.55 on ImageNet 256 × 256 256\times 256 with 725M parameters, the lowest among pixel-space methods. It outperforms mainstream methods with pixel-specialized decoders (PixelDiT-XL, FID 1.61; DiP-XL/16, FID 1.79; DeCo-XL/16, FID 1.69). Notably, RG-L/16 with only 459M parameters (FID 1.79) outperforms JiT-G/16 (2B, FID 1.82) and PixelREPA-H/16 (953M, FID 1.81). At 512 × 512 512\times 512 , we train RG-XL/16 with patch size 16, yielding a 32 × 32 32\times 32 token grid. sections.heading: 4.3 Representation Analysis
sections.text: To understand how RG changes the internal representation, we analyze B/16 models at 200 epochs with PCA visualization and the representation metrics of Section 2 .

sections.heading: Feature visualization.
sections.text: Figure 7 visualizes layer-wise features via PCA. JiT-B shows high-frequency patterns across layers, with unclear contours and noisy object features. REPA clarifies object layout near the aligned layer 4, but later layers revert to high-frequency patterns. RG instead maintains clear semantic contours and foreground–background separation in encoder layers 3–8, while high-frequency patterns dominate decoder layers 9–12, indicating functional specialization.

sections.heading: Effect of each component.
sections.text: Figure 8 shows that the bottleneck improves spatial structure at encoder layer 8 (higher RMSC and LDS), while guidance further strengthens functional specialization and global semantics. We conjecture that amplifying the representation-induced offset increases decoder reliance on the representation, encouraging more semantic encoder features. Figure 7: PCA visualization of layer-wise features. Visualized at t = 0.5 t=0.5 . While REPA-induced structure in JiT-B degrades in later layers, RG-B keeps clear semantic contours in encoder layers 3–8, with high-frequency patterns in decoder layers 9–12, indicating functional specialization. Figure 8: Layer-wise representation metrics in RG-B. The bottleneck (BN) improves spatial diversity and locality at the encoder output (layer 8), while representation guidance further strengthens global semantics, as measured by linear probing, and reinforces encoder–decoder specialization.

sections.heading: 5 Related Work
sections.text: Pixel-Space Generation. Most diffusion models generate images in a compressed latent space. Pixel-space generation directly models RGB images, avoiding the reconstruction bottleneck and preserving fine-grained details. Early work explored scalable pixel-space diffusion, flow-based generation, and autoregressive modeling ( Jabri et al., 2022 ; Kingma & Gao, 2023 ; Hoogeboom et al., 2023 ; Tschannen et al., 2024 ) . Recent transformer-based methods improve generation through patch-level modeling, pixel-level refinement, frequency decomposition, and encoder–decoder architectures ( Li & He, 2026 ; Yu et al., 2026 ; Ma et al., 2026a ; Chen et al., 2026 ) . However, learning semantic representations and synthesizing dense pixels from the same raw input often slows convergence. Our method instead learns a compact internal representation to guide the generative objective during training, without requiring an external encoder at sampling time. Representation Learning for Generation. Pretrained visual encoders provide semantic representations that transfer well to recognition tasks, but may discard the fine-grained information needed for image synthesis. Prior work uses these representations as diffusion latents ( Yao et al., 2025 ; Zheng et al., 2026a ) or aligns intermediate diffusion features with frozen encoder features ( Yu et al., 2024 ; Shin et al., 2026 ) . Dedicated encoder–decoder architectures also separate semantic modeling from pixel synthesis ( Wang et al., 2025a ; Ma et al., 2026a ; Chen et al., 2026 ) . While semantic representations can improve optimization, stronger alignment does not necessarily improve generation, and external representations may be mismatched with pixel-level synthesis. Our method learns representations end-to-end under the generative objective: a bottleneck encourages compact features, while representation guidance strengthens their role in generation, preserving global structure and fine-grained pixel information. Guidance in Diffusion Models. Guidance is widely used to steer diffusion models toward conditional distributions. Classifier guidance uses auxiliary classifier gradients, while classifier-free guidance combines conditional and unconditional predictions during sampling ( Dhariwal & Nichol, 2021 ; Ho & Salimans, 2022 ) . Recent work leverages internal predictions: Internal Guidance introduces auxiliary intermediate-layer supervision and extrapolates between intermediate and final predictions during sampling ( Zhou et al., 2026 ) . RAEv2 shows that reparameterizing the REPA prediction head enables self-guidance without a separately trained guidance model or an additional classifier-free forward pass ( Singh et al., 2026 ; Zu et al., 2026 ) . While these methods primarily guide sampling, our representation guidance modifies the flow-matching target during training using the model’s own representation. Gradients propagate through this representation, directly shaping both the learned vector field and the internal features used for generation. Appendix A.3 compares RG with autoguidance ( Karras et al., 2024 ) and Internal Guidance in pixel space.

sections.heading: 6 Conclusion
sections.text: We presented Representation Guidance (RG), which guides pixel diffusion transformers with their own learned representations. RG combines a low-dimensional bottleneck with a representation-guided flow-matching target to strengthen the generative utility of internal features while preserving a plain Transformer architecture. It achieves FIDs of 1.55 and 1.74 on ImageNet 256 × 256 256\times 256 and 512 × 512 512\times 512 , respectively, and extends to text-to-image generation. Our findings highlight that useful generative representations must be both properly formed and actively exploited.

sections.heading: Limitations.
sections.text: Our experiments focus on image generation, and extending RG to larger model scales, video generation, and other modalities such as 3D and audio is left for future work.

sections.heading: A.2 Analysis of Representation Guidance
sections.text: We derive the solution of the RG objective in Eq. ( 5 ) and relate it to CFG. Appendix A.3 compares RG with autoguidance and Internal Guidance.

sections.heading: Training objective.
sections.text: The RG loss replaces the flow matching target with 𝐯 RG \mathbf{v}_{\text{RG}} : ℒ RG = 𝔼 𝐱 , ϵ , t ​ ‖ 𝐯 θ ​ ( 𝐳 t , t , 𝐫 ) − 𝐯 RG ‖ 2 2 . \mathcal{L}_{\text{RG}}=\mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{x},\bm{\epsilon},t}\big\|\mathbf{v}_{\theta}(\mathbf{z}_{t},t,\mathbf{r})-\mathbf{v}_{\text{RG}}\big\|_{2}^{2}. (6) Extrapolating along Δ ​ 𝐯 rep \Delta\mathbf{v}_{\text{rep}} at sampling time as in CFG (Eq. ( 3 )) would double the decoder cost and leave the representation unchanged; RG instead moves guidance into the training target.

sections.heading: Solution of the objective.
sections.text: Let 𝐯 ¯ 𝐫 = 𝔼 [ 𝐯 ∣ 𝐳 t , 𝐫 ] \bar{\mathbf{v}}_{\mathbf{r}}=\mathbb{E}[\mathbf{v}\mid\mathbf{z}_{t},\mathbf{r}] and 𝐯 ¯ ∅ = 𝔼 ⁡ [ 𝐯 ∣ 𝐳 t ] \bar{\mathbf{v}}_{\varnothing}=\mathbb{E}[\mathbf{v}\mid\mathbf{z}_{t}] . Samples with a dropped representation use the plain target, so the representation-free branch converges to 𝐯 ¯ ∅ \bar{\mathbf{v}}_{\varnothing} . Assume that the EMA teacher matches the online network at convergence. The minimizer of Eq. ( 6 ) then satisfies 𝐯 θ ​ ( 𝐳 t , t , 𝐫 ) = 𝐯 ¯ 𝐫 + ( s − 1 ) ​ ( 𝐯 θ ​ ( 𝐳 t , t , 𝐫 ) − 𝐯 ¯ ∅ ) \mathbf{v}_{\theta}(\mathbf{z}_{t},t,\mathbf{r})=\bar{\mathbf{v}}_{\mathbf{r}}+(s-1)\big(\mathbf{v}_{\theta}(\mathbf{z}_{t},t,\mathbf{r})-\bar{\mathbf{v}}_{\varnothing}\big) , which gives 𝐯 θ ​ ( 𝐳 t , t , 𝐫 ) = 𝐯 ¯ ∅ + 1 2 − s ​ ( 𝐯 ¯ 𝐫 − 𝐯 ¯ ∅ ) , 1 ≤ s < 2 . \mathbf{v}_{\theta}(\mathbf{z}_{t},t,\mathbf{r})=\bar{\mathbf{v}}_{\varnothing}+\frac{1}{2-s}\big(\bar{\mathbf{v}}_{\mathbf{r}}-\bar{\mathbf{v}}_{\varnothing}\big),\qquad 1\leq s<2. (7) RG therefore trains the network to output a CFG-style velocity with an effective scale w rep = 1 / ( 2 − s ) w_{\text{rep}}=1/(2-s) , where the representation acts as the condition. For s = 1.4 s=1.4 , w rep ≈ 1.67 w_{\text{rep}}\approx 1.67 . By analogy with CFG, this informally corresponds to the sharpened distribution p ⁡ ( 𝐳 t ) ​ p ​ ( 𝐫 ∣ 𝐳 t ) w rep p(\mathbf{z}_{t})\,p(\mathbf{r}\mid\mathbf{z}_{t})^{w_{\text{rep}}} , which concentrates on samples consistent with the learned representation. Since part of the guidance is built into the model, a larger s s reduces the CFG scale needed at sampling time (Section 4.4 ).

sections.heading: Effect on the representation.
sections.text: CFG and MG use a fixed condition, whereas the condition of RG is learned. To fit the shifted target, the representation-conditioned branch must deviate further from the representation-free branch. This requires 𝐫 \mathbf{r} to carry more information useful for denoising. The gradient of ℒ RG \mathcal{L}_{\text{RG}} flows through 𝐫 \mathbf{r} into the bottleneck and the encoder. RG therefore increases the dependence of the decoder on the representation and shapes the representation for generation.

sections.text: Autoguidance ( Karras et al., 2024 ) , Internal Guidance (IG) ( Zhou et al., 2026 ) , and RG all guide a model with a weaker version of itself, extrapolating from a weak prediction toward the full one. How the weak prediction is obtained determines what the guidance amplifies (Table 10 , top). Table 10: Self-guidance methods. Top: how each method obtains its weak prediction. sections.heading: Connections.
sections.text: Autoguidance obtains the weak prediction from a separately trained model with reduced capacity or training, and extrapolates at sampling time. IG attaches an auxiliary output head to an intermediate block, supervises it with the flow matching loss, and extrapolates from this shallow prediction toward the final one. Its training-time variant adds ω ​ sg ⁡ ( 𝐯 final − 𝐯 inter ) \omega\,\operatorname{sg}(\mathbf{v}_{\text{final}}-\mathbf{v}_{\text{inter}}) to the flow matching target, the same form as Eq. ( 5 ). RG admits a similar view. Since 𝐫 \mathbf{r} is computed from 𝐳 t \mathbf{z}_{t} , Δ ​ 𝐯 rep \Delta\mathbf{v}_{\text{rep}} is the difference between the full model and its representation-free sub-network, i.e., the decoder without access to the encoder.

sections.heading: Differences.
sections.text: The weak prediction of autoguidance lacks capacity, and that of IG lacks depth. The weak prediction of RG lacks only the information carried by 𝐫 \mathbf{r} : both branches share the decoder, the input, the time, and the condition. Δ ​ 𝐯 rep \Delta\mathbf{v}_{\text{rep}} therefore isolates the contribution of a compact learned representation, whereas the offsets of autoguidance and IG contain every difference between two predictors. RG also differs in what training optimizes. In autoguidance and IG, the guidance direction is a by-product of separately supervised predictions. In RG, the gradient of ℒ RG \mathcal{L}_{\text{RG}} flows through 𝐫 \mathbf{r} into the encoder, so training shapes the representation that defines the guidance. RG needs neither a second model nor an auxiliary head, and adds no inference cost.

sections.heading: Internal Guidance in pixel space.
sections.text: IG was developed for latent diffusion transformers, SiT and LightningDiT on VAE latents with 𝐯 \mathbf{v} -prediction. We apply its training-time variant to JiT-B/16 following the IG paper: an auxiliary head after block 4, an auxiliary loss weight of 0.5, ω = 0.5 \omega=0.5 from epoch 20, EMA predictions, no guidance interval, and no REPA. We train for 200 epochs and evaluate as in Section 4.4 . IG raises the FID of JiT-B from 4.56 to 5.22 and lowers IS (Table 10 , bottom). Its optimal CFG scale drops from 3.3 to 2.4, so part of the guidance is absorbed into the model, but this does not improve generation. Under the same comparison, RG reduces the FID from 3.79 to 3.28 and similarly lowers the optimal CFG scale from 3.95 to 2.60. Figure 11: Layer-wise representation of RG-B, JiT-B, and JiT-B with IG. The shaded band marks block 4, where IG attaches its auxiliary output head. IG collapses spatial structure at this block and leaves global semantics unchanged.

sections.heading: Why IG is less effective in pixel space.
sections.text: Measured with the metrics of Section 2 (Figure 11 ), JiT-B with IG meets neither requirement identified there. The representation is not properly formed. The auxiliary head forces block 4 to predict pixels directly, which imposes pixel-level pressure on an intermediate layer. At this block, RMSC drops from 0.46 to 0.28 and LDS from 0.11 to 0.04 relative to JiT-B, and linear probing accuracy falls from 21.2% at layer 3 to 19.1%. Layers 5–8 remain less spatially structured than in JiT-B (RMSC 0.34–0.45 vs. 0.46–0.48), and the peak probing accuracy is unchanged (29.1% vs. 29.5%). The auxiliary supervision thus pulls intermediate features toward pixel synthesis, the same tendency that erodes externally aligned semantics in Section 2 . The guidance does not exploit a representation. In pixel space with 𝐱 \mathbf{x} -prediction, the shallow prediction is almost as accurate as the full one. At the end of training, the auxiliary head reaches a flow matching loss of 0.0696, only 4% above the 0.0667 of the final output, and the RMS of 𝐯 final − 𝐯 inter \mathbf{v}_{\text{final}}-\mathbf{v}_{\text{inter}} is 0.107. The remaining eight blocks add a small residual. We conjecture that this residual mainly consists of fine pixel detail rather than semantics or layout, consistent with the high-frequency features of pixel models (Figure 7 ). Amplifying it does not strengthen global structure. In latent space, where the VAE removes most pixel detail, this gap more likely reflects semantic refinement.

sections.heading: How RG addresses both issues.
sections.text: RG changes what defines the weak prediction and where the representation is formed. First, 𝐫 \mathbf{r} is formed at a compact bottleneck and is never asked to reproduce pixels. The decoder handles pixel synthesis from 𝐳 t \mathbf{z}_{t} through its own patch embedding. The RG-B encoder therefore keeps high spatial diversity and locality (RMSC up to 0.91, LDS up to 0.66) and reaches 55.2% probing accuracy, nearly twice that of JiT-B and JiT-B with IG. Second, Δ ​ 𝐯 rep \Delta\mathbf{v}_{\text{rep}} removes only 𝐫 \mathbf{r} , so its magnitude reflects how much the decoder relies on the representation rather than how much depth adds. Guidance thus amplifies the semantic and structural content carried by 𝐫 \mathbf{r} , and its gradient further improves 𝐫 \mathbf{r} . The component ablation (Table 8 ) confirms that guidance helps only when the representation is well formed. Without REPA and the bottleneck, guidance raises the FID to 8.08. With both, it lowers the FID from 3.79 to 3.28. Finally, unlike IG, RG skips highly noisy inputs; applying it at all noise levels raises the FID to 5.28 (Figure 9 (b)).

sections.heading: A.4 Representation Metrics
sections.text: All representation metrics are computed with the EMA weights at epoch 200. For each model, we extract the output tokens of every transformer block and exclude the in-context class tokens. For decoupled models, layers 1–8 refer to the encoder blocks and layers 9–12 refer to the decoder blocks. Each block output contains N = 256 N=256 patch tokens of dimension D = 768 D=768 .

sections.heading: RMSC.
sections.text: We follow Singh et al. (2025) . Let 𝐡 1 , … , 𝐡 N \mathbf{h}_{1},\dots,\mathbf{h}_{N} be the patch tokens of one image, and let 𝐡 ^ i = 𝐡 i / ‖ 𝐡 i ‖ 2 \hat{\mathbf{h}}_{i}=\mathbf{h}_{i}/\|\mathbf{h}_{i}\|_{2} . RMSC is defined as RMSC = ( 1 N ​ ∑ i = 1 N ‖ 𝐡 ^ i − 𝐡 ¯ ‖ 2 2 ) 1 / 2 , 𝐡 ¯ = 1 N ​ ∑ i = 1 N 𝐡 ^ i . \mathrm{RMSC}=\Big(\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\big\|\hat{\mathbf{h}}_{i}-\bar{\mathbf{h}}\big\|_{2}^{2}\Big)^{1/2},\qquad\bar{\mathbf{h}}=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\hat{\mathbf{h}}_{i}. (8) A higher RMSC means that the tokens of different spatial positions are more distinct. We compute RMSC on the 50K ImageNet validation images and average it over images.

sections.heading: LDS.
sections.text: Local-vs-distant similarity (LDS) ( Singh et al., 2025 ) measures the contrast between nearby and distant patch tokens. Using the normalized tokens defined above, we compute LDS = 1 | 𝒩 | ​ ∑ ( i , j ) ∈ 𝒩 𝐡 ^ i ⊤ ​ 𝐡 ^ j − 1 | ℱ | ​ ∑ ( i , j ) ∈ ℱ 𝐡 ^ i ⊤ ​ 𝐡 ^ j . \mathrm{LDS}=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{N}|}\sum_{(i,j)\in\mathcal{N}}\hat{\mathbf{h}}_{i}^{\top}\hat{\mathbf{h}}_{j}-\frac{1}{|\mathcal{F}|}\sum_{(i,j)\in\mathcal{F}}\hat{\mathbf{h}}_{i}^{\top}\hat{\mathbf{h}}_{j}. (9) On the 16 × 16 16\times 16 patch grid, 𝒩 \mathcal{N} contains horizontal and vertical neighbors, and ℱ \mathcal{F} contains pairs with Manhattan distance at least 6. A higher LDS indicates greater local similarity relative to distant positions. We compute LDS per image and average it over the 50K validation images. For both RMSC and LDS, the input is the noisy image 𝐳 t = t ​ 𝐱 + ( 1 − t ) ​ ϵ \mathbf{z}_{t}=t\,\mathbf{x}+(1-t)\,\bm{\epsilon} with the ground-truth class label, and the representation is always kept. We compute the metrics at t ∈ { 0.1 , 0.3 , 0.5 , 0.7 , 0.9 } t\in\{0.1,0.3,0.5,0.7,0.9\} and report their average. All models share the same images and noise.

sections.heading: Linear probing.
sections.text: We feed clean images ( t = 1 t=1 ) with the null class label to the model, and average the patch tokens of each block to obtain image-level features. For each layer, we train a linear classifier on the features of the ImageNet training set, preceded by a BatchNorm layer without affine parameters. We use Adam with a learning rate of 10 − 3 10^{-3} , cosine decay, a batch size of 16384, and 90 epochs. We report the top-1 accuracy on the ImageNet validation set.

sections.heading: CFG sweeps.
sections.text: Figure 12 shows the FID of B/16 models at epoch 200 under different CFG scales. For each RG setting, we report the FID over the evaluated range of CFG scales. The CFG interval is ( 0.1 , 1 ] (0.1,1] in all cases. A larger RG scale shifts the optimal CFG scale to smaller values, which is consistent with Eq. ( 7 ). When RG is applied at all noise levels ( t min = 0 t_{\min}=0 ), the FID remains high for all CFG scales. Figure 12: FID versus CFG scale at epoch 200. (a) Different RG scales s s . (b) Different lower bounds t min t_{\min} of the RG interval. Larger RG scales favor smaller CFG scales.

sections.heading: Guidance teacher.
sections.text: By default, RG computes Δ ​ 𝐯 rep \Delta\mathbf{v}_{\text{rep}} with the EMA network (Section 3.3 ). We also train RG-B with the online network as the teacher and keep the stop-gradient and all other settings. Both teachers use two gradient-free forward passes, and the EMA weights are maintained for sampling in either case, so the training cost is identical. As shown in Figure 13 , the online teacher lowers the FID at every CFG scale, from 3.28 to 3.18 at the respective optimum, and raises IS from 264.1 to 272.3. The gap grows with the CFG scale, from 0.02 at 2.0 to 0.12 at 2.8. We attribute this gain to the learned condition of RG. MG guides with a fixed class label, so an EMA teacher only smooths the prediction. In RG, the condition 𝐫 \mathbf{r} is itself learned and changes during training. With a decay of 0.9999, the EMA network averages over roughly 10 4 10^{4} steps, or about eight epochs, so its offset describes an earlier representation rather than the 𝐫 \mathbf{r} that conditions the student. The online teacher evaluates Eq. ( 5 ) exactly as written, with the same parameters for the teacher and the student, and the target always reflects the current representation. The stop-gradient treats this offset as a constant at each step, which suffices to keep training stable in our setting. Both results come from single runs. The consistent gap across CFG scales suggests a systematic effect, but all other results in this paper use the EMA teacher.

sections.heading: Warm-up length.
sections.text: By default, RG is enabled after 20 epochs of plain flow matching. Enabling it at epoch 0, 10, or 30 instead changes the FID by less than 0.01 (Figure 13 , right), a far smaller effect than that of the RG scale or interval (Figure 9 ). RG is thus insensitive to the warm-up length. It even works when enabled from the first epoch, while the EMA teacher is still close to its initialization. We conjecture that the representation carries little information early in training, so Δ ​ 𝐯 rep \Delta\mathbf{v}_{\text{rep}} is small and RG stays close to plain flow matching. The guidance then grows as the representation becomes informative. The warm-up is therefore optional, and we keep 20 epochs as the default. sections.heading: Convergence.
sections.text: Figure 14 compares the FID of RG-B, JiT-B, and JiT-B with REPA during training. REPA speeds up JiT-B in early training, but the advantage disappears after about 160 epochs. RG-B has a lower FID than both models from 100 epochs on, and the margin remains at 200 epochs. With longer training, RG-B matches the 600-epoch FID of JiT-B (3.66) after only 150 epochs, a 4 × 4\times speed-up, and continues to improve to 2.64 at 600 epochs. Figure 14: FID during training. RG-B matches the 600-epoch FID of JiT-B (3.66) after only 150 epochs (3.64), a 4 × 4\times training speed-up. REPA accelerates JiT-B early but is overtaken by the baseline, whereas RG-B keeps improving to 2.64 at 600 epochs.

sections.heading: Layer-wise comparison with JiT.
sections.text: Figure 15 compares RG-B with JiT-B and JiT-B with REPA. In JiT-B, the linear probing accuracy increases slowly with depth and peaks at 29.5% at layer 8, and the LDS stays below 0.12 in all layers. REPA raises the accuracy of JiT-B to 60.7% at layer 4, but the accuracy then decreases to 30.8% at layer 12, and the LDS decreases from 0.662 to 0.025. The later layers of JiT convert the aligned features into pixels and gradually discard the semantic information. In RG-B, the linear probing accuracy stays between 52.1% and 55.2% from layer 3 to layer 8 and drops to between 22.7% and 29.2% in the decoder. The last encoder layer has an RMSC of 0.858 and an LDS of 0.390, compared with 0.476 and 0.111 in JiT-B. The encoder thus maintains a semantic and spatially diverse representation up to the interface, and the decoder performs pixel synthesis. JiT-B with REPA has a higher peak accuracy than RG-B, yet RG-B achieves a much lower FID (3.28 vs. 4.80). Generation quality therefore depends on whether the representation is maintained until the decoder uses it, rather than on the peak alignment quality. Report Issue Back to Abstract Download PDF Contents Reading mode Colour theme License: arXiv.org perpetual non-exclusive license arXiv:2610.12978v1 [cs.CV] 09 Oct 2026 Learning Representations to Guide Pixel Diffusion Transformers Zihao Pan 1,2,3 Mengting Chen 2 † \dagger Cheng Shi 3 Taihang Hu 2 Zhengrong Yue 4 Affiliation: Zikang Wang 4 Yuan Wang 2 Wei Li 2 Sibei Yang 1 Affiliation: 1 Sun Yat-sen University 2 Alibaba Group 3 The University of Hong Kong 4 Shanghai Jiao Tong University Affiliation: panzh33@mail2.sysu.edu.cn, cmt271286@taobao.com yangsb3@mail.sysu.edu.cn Affiliation: † \dagger Project leader Corresponding author Abstract Visual representations are largely developed for understanding, yet what makes them useful for generation remains unclear. We study this question in pixel diffusion transformers and uncover two key insights. First, better representation quality does not necessarily translate into greater generative utility, as externally aligned semantics can be progressively lost during pixel synthesis. Second, architectural separation with specialized pixel decoders mainly redistributes semantic and spatial modeling, without necessarily yielding representations better suited to generation. These insights suggest that a useful generative representation must be both properly formed and actively exploited . Motivated by these insights, we introduce Representation Guidance (RG) , which directly forms and exploits internal representations while retaining a plain Transformer architecture. A low-dimensional bottleneck forces generation-relevant information into a compact representation, which is then explicitly used to guide decoder generation by modifying the flow-matching target according to its induced prediction offset. RG learns clearer semantic and spatial structure while scaling efficiently in both parameters and computation. On ImageNet 256 × 256 256\times 256 , RG-L/16 with only 459M parameters outperforms substantially larger pixel diffusion transformers, while RG-XL/16 achieves an FID of 1.55. RG further reaches an FID of 1.74 at 512 × 512 512\times 512 and extends to text-to-image generation, achieving 0.89 on GenEval and 87.1 on DPG-Bench. Figure 1: High-quality pixel-space generation with a plain Transformer. RG guides generation with its learned representations, achieving strong performance in both class-conditional and text-to-image synthesis. We show samples at resolutions from 256 × 256 256\times 256 to 1024 × 1024 1024\times 1024 . 1 Introduction Representation learning has been a central theme in computer vision ( Chen et al., 2020 ; He et al., 2020 ; Caron et al., 2021 ; He et al., 2022 ) . By transforming pixels into structured features, modern vision models have learned representations that transfer effectively across recognition tasks such as classification, detection, and segmentation ( Oquab et al., 2023 ; Siméoni et al., 2025 ) . Yet visual representations have been developed predominantly for understanding. Whether the same notion of a “good representation” applies to generation remains much less clear. Unlike recognition, which can discard much of the low-level image content once semantics are extracted, generation must organize global semantics and spatial structure while ultimately recovering every pixel. This raises a fundamental question: what makes a representation useful for visual generation? Figure 2: Our RG enables efficient scaling and better internal representations. (a) RG scales consistently from B to XL. It achieves lower FID with fewer parameters and FLOPs than plain-Transformer JiT baselines, while also outperforming pixel-specialized decoders at lower complexity. (b) RG learns clearer spatial structure and more localized semantic correspondence. Recent generative models have increasingly borrowed representations from pretrained vision encoders. One line of work improves the latent space in which generation operates, either by aligning autoencoder latents with pretrained features ( Yao et al., 2025 ; Leng et al., 2025 ; Yue et al., 2026 ) or by directly using such features as generative latents ( Zheng et al., 2026a ; Shi et al., 2026b ; Singh et al., 2026 ) . Another line aligns intermediate generative features with pretrained representations ( Yu et al., 2024 ; Wu et al., 2025 ; Wang et al., 2025b ; Singh et al., 2025 ) . While these approaches show that semantic representations can facilitate generative learning, they largely focus on what information a representation contains . For generation, this is only part of the problem: a representation may encode rich semantic and spatial structure, yet provide limited benefit if it is not properly formed for synthesis or if the generative process does not actually exploit it. We study this problem in pixel diffusion transformers (pDiTs) ( Chen et al., 2025c ; Yu et al., 2026 ) , where representation learning and image synthesis take place end-to-end from raw pixels rather than through a representation space predefined by an external autoencoder ( Rombach et al., 2022 ) . More importantly, JiT ( Li & He, 2026 ) shows that competitive pixel generation can be achieved with a plain Transformer, providing a simple setting for examining how internal representations emerge and interact with pixel synthesis. Our analysis of this setting reveals two key insights. • First, better representation quality does not necessarily translate into greater generative utility. Aligning an intermediate JiT layer with DINOv2 ( Oquab et al., 2023 ) substantially improves its semantic and spatial structure at the aligned layer. However, these gains rapidly diminish in subsequent layers as the network approaches pixel prediction. The same mismatch appears in generation: REPA ( Yu et al., 2024 ) accelerates early training, but the baseline eventually overtakes it, while moving the alignment deeper further degrades the final FID. These results show that simply injecting stronger semantics is insufficient—a representation benefits generation only when its information is preserved and remains functionally relevant to subsequent synthesis. • Second, architectural separation does not necessarily improve representation for generation; it mainly redistributes semantic and spatial modeling across the network. A natural response is to separate representation learning from pixel synthesis with an additional specialized pixel decoder ( Yu et al., 2026 ; Ma et al., 2026a ; Chen et al., 2026 ) . However, the decoder itself reshapes the encoder representation: its spatial modeling capacity determines what the encoder must retain, producing different balances of global semantics and spatial structure without yielding a representation better suited to generation. These designs also incur substantial parameter and computation overhead. Thus, they mainly shift the modeling burden between encoder and decoder while departing from JiT’s simple, scalable Transformer design. Figure 3: Architecture comparison. Together, these findings suggest that a useful generative representation must be both properly formed and actively exploited . It should emerge through a compact interface that encourages the model to organize information into a concise, generation-relevant representation, while remaining tightly coupled to subsequent synthesis. Neither alone is sufficient: forcing the generator to rely on a poorly formed representation can amplify unhelpful low-level information, whereas a well-structured representation provides little benefit if it can be ignored. Based on these insights, we introduce Representation Guidance (RG) . RG preserves a plain Transformer architecture and operates on the representation interface rather than introducing a specialized pixel decoder. First, a low-dimensional bottleneck between the encoder and decoder forms a compact implicit latent space, encouraging generation-relevant information to be organized into a concise internal representation. Second, RG explicitly strengthens the generative utility of this representation. We compare decoder predictions with and without the representation and use the resulting representation-induced velocity offset to modify the flow-matching target ( Lipman et al., 2023 ; Liu et al., 2023 ; Albergo & Vanden-Eijnden, 2023 ) . This increases the model’s dependence on the representation, while gradients through it simultaneously shape the encoder toward information useful for synthesis. The bottleneck and guidance thus play complementary roles: the former governs how the representation is formed , while the latter ensures that generation actually uses it . Pretrained representation alignment thus provides a semantic scaffold, while the representation consumed by the decoder is ultimately learned end-to-end for generation. RG also shares a core principle with self-distillation in self-supervised learning ( Caron et al., 2021 ; Oquab et al., 2023 ) : the representation is bootstrapped from targets derived from the model’s own predictions. Whereas self-distillation sharpens the teacher distribution to induce discriminative features, RG sharpens the velocity target along the representation-induced offset, which compels the representation to encode the semantic and spatial structure required for generation (Figure 6 ). Figure 2 summarizes the consequences of this representation-centered design. Without introducing specialized pixel modules, RG achieves a substantially stronger parameter–quality and compute–quality trade-off, scales consistently with model size, and develops markedly clearer semantic and spatial organization in its internal representations. On ImageNet ( Deng et al., 2009 ) 256 × 256 256\times 256 , RG-XL/16 achieves an FID of 1.55, while RG-L/16 reaches 1.79 with only 459M parameters, outperforming substantially larger pixel-space models. RG further achieves an FID of 1.74 at 512 × 512 512\times 512 and extends naturally to text-to-image generation, reaching 0.89 on GenEval ( Ghosh et al., 2023 ) and 87.1 on DPG-Bench ( Hu et al., 2024 ) . These results show that effective representation learning in pixel diffusion does not require increasingly elaborate pixel decoders or ever-stronger externally imposed features. Instead, a plain Transformer can learn representations that benefit generation when the representation is both properly formed and explicitly exploited. 2 What Makes Representations Useful in pDiTs? Most diffusion models generate images in a compressed latent space. Pixel-space generation directly models RGB images, avoiding the reconstruction bottleneck and preserving fine-grained details. Early work explored scalable pixel-space diffusion, flow-based generation, and autoregressive modeling ( Jabri et al., 2022 ; Kingma & Gao, 2023 ; Hoogeboom et al., 2023 ; Tschannen et al., 2024 ) . Recent transformer-based methods improve generation through patch-level modeling, pixel-level refinement, frequency decomposition, and encoder–decoder architectures ( Li & He, 2026 ; Yu et al., 2026 ; Ma et al., 2026a ; Chen et al., 2026 ) . However, learning semantic representations and synthesizing dense pixels from the same raw input often slows convergence. Our method instead learns a compact internal representation to guide the generative objective during training, without requiring an external encoder at sampling time. Representation Learning for Generation. Pretrained visual encoders provide semantic representations that transfer well to recognition tasks, but may discard the fine-grained information needed for image synthesis. Prior work uses these representations as diffusion latents ( Yao et al., 2025 ; Zheng et al., 2026a ) or aligns intermediate diffusion features with frozen encoder features ( Yu et al., 2024 ; Shin et al., 2026 ) . Dedicated encoder–decoder architectures also separate semantic modeling from pixel synthesis ( Wang et al., 2025a ; Ma et al., 2026a ; Chen et al., 2026 ) . While semantic representations can improve optimization, stronger alignment does not necessarily improve generation, and external representations may be mismatched with pixel-level synthesis. Our method learns representations end-to-end under the generative objective: a bottleneck encourages compact features, while representation guidance strengthens their role in generation, preserving global structure and fine-grained pixel information.
